EMI causes degradation of electrical equipment performance by inducing unwanted currents and voltages.
EMI sources include natural phenomena like cosmic rays and solar flares, and man-made sources such as mobile phones and power cables.
EMI measurement is divided into emission testing (measuring noise emitted) and immunity testing (measuring device tolerance).
Open Area Test Sites (OATS) typically use distances of 3 to 10 meters between EUT and receiving antenna for radiated emission testing.
Anechoic chambers use microwave absorbers to create reflection-free environments for EMI testing.
Reverberation chambers create statistically uniform electromagnetic fields using metallic stirrers for faster immunity testing.
GTEM cells provide a compact, affordable alternative for EMI testing from 0 Hz to 20 GHz.
Line Impedance Stabilization Networks (LISNs) stabilize power line impedance and enable conducted emission measurements up to 100 MHz.
Continuous immunity testing includes magnetic field immunity using Helmholtz coils and radiated immunity per IEC 61000-4-3.
EMI reduction techniques include electromagnetic shielding, EMI filters, circuit topology modifications, and spread spectrum methods.
Early EMI testing reduces production costs by identifying issues before expensive compliance testing.
Radiated emission testing frequency range commonly spans 30 MHz to 1 GHz.
MIMO system EMI can be assessed using two-stage OTA testing involving 3D radiation pattern measurement and channel modeling.
EMI testing standards referenced include CISPR 16, IEC 61000-4-3, IEC 61967-2, and EN 55022.
Shielding effectiveness measures a material's ability to block electromagnetic interference.
Conducted emission testing measures noise on power lines emitted by the EUT.
The EUT is oriented sequentially in three orthogonal directions during GTEM cell testing to ensure compliance.
Reverberation chambers do not require mechanical rotation of the EUT due to their statistically uniform fields.
EMI immunity testing assesses whether the device functions correctly when exposed to electromagnetic disturbances.
The paper emphasizes the lack of comprehensive EMI/EMC literature covering all aspects of the field.
